sections.title: The CIPS Examination at a Glance

blocks.text: The Certified Interventional Pain Sonologist (CIPS) examination, administered by the World Institute of Pain (WIP) Board of Examination together with the World Academy of Pain Medicine Ultrasonography (WAPMU), certifies physicians in ultrasound-guided interventional pain techniques. It is administered in English (except part 2B) and consists of three parts:

head: Part
Format
Duration
Weight
rows: 100 four-option multiple-choice questions covering general ultrasound knowledge, chronic pain, spine, peripheral/autonomic nerves and musculoskeletal topics
Four ultrasound-guided procedures on a fresh cadaver, one from each region (spine, MSK joint, MSK soft tissue, peripheral nerve), before two examiners
One extended clinical vignette: 5 minutes to review, then diagnosis and procedure questions (up to 10), plus a physical and ultrasound examination of a live model

blocks.text: The final score is a criterion-referenced weighted composite (practical 60%, oral 20%, written 20%). Practical and oral components are scored on a four-point scale: 1 = unacceptable, potentially dangerous; 2 = unacceptable but not harmful; 3 = acceptable, basic competence; 4 = acceptable, exceeds basic competence. Passing is based on performance across all three components; it is not curved against other candidates.

items: Results are e-mailed approximately eight weeks after the examination; passing candidates receive a pass letter only (no numeric score), while failing candidates receive a score and a diagnostic report per part.
There is no limit on retakes, but after three failures the candidate must complete one additional year of practice before reapplying.
Appeals: a written request for hand rescoring within 20 calendar days of the score report, with a USD 50 fee; the hand-scored result is final.

Eligibility: unrestricted medical license; completed ACGME-accredited (or equivalent) residency including pain management; ABMS board certification or national equivalent; documented ultrasound training (residency/fellowship or 20 Category-1 CME credits in approved courses such as WAPMU, ASRA, ESRA, ISURA, ISSPS); and at least 12 months of pain medicine practice after residency (a 12-month pain fellowship counts).

Application: online via the eCIPS system (http://bit.ly/cipsapp), fee USD 2,500; two physician recommendation letters (only one from a partner; none from relatives); credential review takes about four weeks once the file is complete.

Refunds: the fee is refunded (minus USD 250 administration fee) only if the Board finds you ineligible. Rescheduling incurs a USD 100 fee; you must sit an exam within 2 years or 4 exam cycles of the original application.
On exam day bring photo identification and arrive about 45 minutes early; late arrivals are not admitted. Phones, smart devices, books, paper, food and beverages are prohibited in the testing room.

blocks.text: For each of the four cadaver procedures, each examiner answers eight checklist questions and then assigns an overall 1-4 rating. Aim to earn a clear yes on every item:

items: Did the examinee appropriately use the ultrasound machine? (correct mode, depth, gain, focus, frequency adjustments)
Did the examinee choose the proper equipment? (transducer type, needle gauge/length, sterile supplies)
Did the examinee correctly use the probe? (orientation, handling, cable management, stability)
Did the examinee correctly identify the anatomic target(s)?
Did the examinee appropriately use ultrasound as a guide? (real-time guidance rather than blind technique)
Did the examinee demonstrate acceptable skin entry for the needle?
Did the examinee visualize the needle tip before advancing the needle? - the single most emphasized safety behavior
Did the examinee correctly position the needle at the end position?

blocks.text: Overall rating logic: first decide acceptable versus unacceptable, then fine-grade - 4 means flawless technique that maximizes effectiveness and minimizes complications; 3 means minor errors only; 2 means major errors with temporary, non-harmful consequences; 1 means dangerous errors risking permanent harm.
The modified oral examination uses one vignette. Expect this fixed sequence of question areas (from the examiner rating form):

items: Possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis).

Physical examination of the live model - scored separately on positioning, a neurological examination with tools (reflex hammer, tuning fork, toothpick, brush are provided), and an MSK examination covering active and passive range of motion, tone, power, circumference/diameter, and named special tests.
Diagnostic tests to order or perform.

Ultrasound examination - scored against a 12-item checklist: machine placed ergonomically; patient/physician information entered on the record; correct settings chosen and adapted during the exam; correct transducer; transducer cleaned before/after; gloves used; regional overview first; exam focused on the target; measurements taken and compared with the contralateral side; color Doppler or power Doppler used; dynamic examination performed; and ability to name pointed-out structures.
Best conservative treatment options.
Best interventional technique.
Description of the procedure (stepwise, with doses and volumes).
Potential complications and side effects.
Major attention points in post-procedure evaluation.

blocks.text: Oral answers are rated 1-4: a 4 requires accurate, complete knowledge of pathophysiology, indications, contraindications and complications reflecting current practice standards; a 1 reflects knowledge gaps that could produce grossly negligent or dangerous care.

items: Use the 5-minute preparation period: plan the order of your four procedures so the cadaver is turned as little as possible, as the examiners will instruct.
Narrate while you work: name the transducer, settings, structures, and needle view. Examiners can only score what they observe, and a silent candidate hides competence.
Never advance the needle without seeing the tip - if you lose the tip, stop, withdraw to a known view, and re-acquire. This single behavior separates a 3-4 from a 1.
Treat the model and cadaver like a real patient: gloves, probe cleaning, PPE, ergonomic machine position, patient information entered before scanning.
Respect the clock: 15 minutes per procedure, up to 30 minutes for the whole oral case including the physical and ultrasound examination.
Do not expect feedback. Examiners are forbidden to teach or to comment on performance; a neutral face is not a failed answer.

intro.text: Two examiners independently score every procedure and every oral answer. They are trained to be neutral: they will not teach, hint, debate, or signal whether your answer is right or wrong, and they rate what you actually do and say - not how confident you appear. Knowing their checklists tells you exactly where marks are earned.

items: Ultrasound is sound above human hearing (greater than 20 kHz); diagnostic imaging uses roughly 2-18 MHz. The transducer converts electrical energy to mechanical (sound) energy and back via the piezoelectric effect.

Frequency trade-off: higher frequency gives better axial resolution but less penetration (attenuation rises with frequency); lower frequency penetrates deeper at the cost of resolution. Always choose the highest frequency that still reaches the target.
Resolution types: axial (along the beam, better with high frequency and short pulses), lateral (across the beam, best at the focal zone), and temporal (frame rate).
Attenuation = absorption + reflection + scattering. Bone reflects and absorbs heavily, producing acoustic shadowing; fluid transmits sound, producing posterior acoustic enhancement.

Echogenicity vocabulary: bone cortex and fascia are hyperechoic; muscle is relatively hypoechoic with hyperechoic perimysium giving a feathery or streaky pattern in longitudinal view; tendon is fibrillar and hyperechoic when the beam is perpendicular; nerve shows a honeycomb (fascicular) pattern in short axis - hypoechoic fascicles in a hyperechoic epineurium.

Linear array (high frequency, about 7-15 MHz): superficial structures - most peripheral nerve and MSK targets. Curvilinear array (low frequency, about 2-6 MHz): deep targets such as the hip, piriformis, lumbar spine and neuraxial structures. Hockey-stick probes help in small parts and tight spaces.

Knobology: set depth so the target occupies the middle third of the screen; place the focal zone at or just below the target; adjust overall gain and time-gain compensation for uniform brightness; select the appropriate frequency/preset; use compound imaging and beam steering to improve needle and tendon visibility.
Orientation convention: keep a consistent probe-marker convention (for example marker cephalad or to the left of the screen) and confirm orientation by sliding or tapping before every needle pass.

Color Doppler displays direction and mean velocity of flow; power Doppler is more sensitive to low flow but has no direction information. Use Doppler before every injection to map vessels along the planned needle path - mandatory near the vertebral artery, deep circumflex iliac artery, suprascapular artery, pudendal vessels and radicular arteries.
Doppler also detects hyperemia (active inflammation, for example in epicondylosis or carpal tunnel syndrome) and confirms injectate spread during caudal epidural injection.
Anisotropy - the key MSK artifact: tendons and nerves turn falsely hypoechoic when the beam is not perpendicular. Correct by toggling/heel-toeing the probe; do not misread anisotropy as tendinopathy.
Posterior acoustic shadowing behind bone and calcifications; posterior acoustic enhancement deep to fluid (vessels, cysts, effusions).
Reverberation and comet-tail artifacts from needles and metallic surfaces; mirror-image artifact at strong reflectors such as the pleura or diaphragm.

In-plane (long-axis) approach: the whole shaft and tip are seen as a hyperechoic line - preferred whenever anatomy allows. Out-of-plane (short-axis) approach: the tip appears as a bright dot only at the moment it crosses the beam; advance in small steps, re-centering the beam on the dot each time.

Improve visibility: steep angles defeat specular reflection, so keep the needle as parallel to the probe face as anatomy permits; use echogenic needles, beam steering, compound imaging, gentle needle jiggling, and inject a tiny test bolus to confirm the tip (hydro-location).
Rule for the practical exam: if the tip is lost, stop advancing - withdraw or re-image until the tip is re-identified.

Aseptic technique: hand hygiene, gloves, skin antisepsis, sterile gel, and transducer cover or probe cleaned/disinfected before and after contact - WAPMU/AIUM standards are explicitly scored in the oral examination.

Ergonomics: position the machine directly in front of you at eye level, the patient within comfortable reach, and adjust the table height to avoid wrist and neck strain; request repositioning of the model or machine when needed - this is scored.

Documentation (AIUM/WAPMU): record patient and physician identification, date, machine settings, labeled images of the target and final needle position, and a brief report of findings with measurements where relevant - for example structure size compared with the contralateral side.

Take a structured history: onset, mechanism of injury, character (nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic), distribution, aggravating/relieving factors, night pain, function, prior treatments and response, and psychosocial flags.
Neuropathic descriptors (burning, shooting, allodynia, numbness) point toward nerve involvement and guide both drug choice and target selection for intervention.

Red flags requiring work-up before injection: trauma with deformity, fever or infection signs, malignancy history, unexplained weight loss, progressive neurological deficit, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and anticoagulation.

Always correlate symptoms with examination and imaging: asymptomatic imaging findings (rotator cuff tears, facet arthrosis, disc degeneration) are common, so diagnostic blocks have a gate-keeping role before destructive treatments.

Stepwise approach: simple analgesics and NSAIDs first; add adjuvants for neuropathic pain (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics); topical agents (lidocaine, capsaicin, NSAIDs) for focal pain; opioids only after risk-benefit assessment with monitoring.

Injectates used in the exam: local anesthetics (lidocaine, bupivacaine) for diagnostic blocks; corticosteroids (triamcinolone 20-40 mg or betamethasone 3-6 mg per typical joint) for therapeutic effect; know steroid side effects - hyperglycemia, skin depigmentation, fat atrophy, flare, tendon weakening with repeated intratendinous exposure.

Anticoagulation management: know which procedures are low versus high risk and the general principle of continuing or holding agents per current interventional pain guidelines; always ask in the vignette.

Standard algorithm: confirm the pain generator with a controlled or comparative diagnostic block before proceeding to a definitive treatment such as radiofrequency ablation; combine interventions with rehabilitation.
Multidisciplinary management: physical therapy, psychological interventions (CBT), occupational therapy, and referral pathways to neurology, neurosurgery or rehabilitation medicine when indicated.

Conservative options to cite in the oral exam: analgesics/NSAIDs, topical agents, TENS, taping/bracing, physical and occupational therapy, and structured exercise - before escalating to injection, PRP or surgery.

intro.text: General principles for spinal sonography: use a curvilinear transducer for the lumbar spine and a high-frequency linear transducer for the cervical region; count levels from reliable landmarks (C2 bifid spinous process, C7 vertebra prominens, the sacrum as a hyperechoic median ridge); always run color Doppler over the needle path to exclude vessels (vertebral artery, radicular branches); and confirm final needle position in two planes whenever possible.

items: Written (20%): work through a full-length MCQ bank by domain; review every error against the anatomy and the key literature statistics cited in this guide.

Practical (60%): rehearse all 20 listed procedures on volunteers or models with a strict 15-minute timer; practice the eight examiner checklist behaviors until they are automatic, especially tip visualization and two-plane confirmation.

Oral (20%): rehearse the 16 vignette topics with a partner playing examiner using the exact 9-question sequence; perform the physical and ultrasound examination aloud, including positioning, neurological examination with tools, measurements compared with the other side, Doppler, and dynamic maneuvers.
Final week: re-read the examiner checklists, review the complication list for every procedure, and sleep before the exam - the practical day is long.

procedures.title: Cervical Medial Branch Block
procedures.target: Diagnostic block for cervical facet-mediated pain; the medial branch is the target for radiofrequency neurotomy.
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus (side up) or prone with the neck slightly flexed; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse (axial) scan over the lateral neck shows the articular pillars as a sawtooth line of hyperechoic peaks; the groove at the waist of the articular pillar between two peaks is the target. The C2 bifid spinous process and C7 vertebra prominens help level counting; the third occipital nerve lies at the C2-3 joint line.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from lateral to medial (or posterior to anterior) with a 22-25 G needle directed to the waist of the articular pillar; confirm the tip on bone in the groove.
procedures.pearls: Check Doppler for the vertebral artery, which runs anteriorly at the level of the foramen; keep the tip against bone. In the coronal scan of the cervical spine, the structures between articular pillars correspond to the cervical medial branch nerves (classic exam image).

procedures.title: Cervical Selective Nerve Root Block
procedures.target: Diagnostic and therapeutic block for cervical radicular pain.
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus or supine with the head turned away; high- frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Axial oblique view: the transverse process shows an anterior and a posterior tubercle (the two-humped camel sign) with the exiting nerve root between them, posterior to the carotid and internal jugular vein; the vertebral artery lies anteriorly at the foramen (typically entering at C6).
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from posterior to anterior, targeting the posterior aspect of the nerve root in the intervertebral foramen; keep the tip outside the foramen proper and use Doppler to exclude radicular and vertebral vessels.
procedures.injectate: Small volume, 0.5-1.0 mL (local anesthetic +/- steroid); inject slowly after negative aspiration.
procedures.pearls: Intravascular injection into the vertebral artery or a radicular artery can cause seizure or spinal cord infarction - real-time visualization of injectate spread is essential; report technical success of ultrasound-guided cervical SNRB is high in experienced hands.

procedures.title: Thoracic Medial Branch / Facet Joint Block
procedures.target: Diagnostic block for thoracic facet-mediated pain.
procedures.position: Prone; low- to mid-frequency curvilinear or linear transducer depending on habitus.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Paramedian sagittal oblique scan: ribs appear as rounded hyperechoic lines with shadowing; between transverse processes the facet joint is seen as a hypoechoic gap between hyperechoic articular processes.
procedures.technique: Described under ultrasound in the sagittal plane with a caudal-to-cephalic in- plane needle approach (Stulic et al., J Ultrasound Med 2011); the tip is walked onto the junction of the transverse process and superior articular process.
procedures.pearls: Stay on bone to avoid pleural injury; the paramedian sagittal oblique view improves joint visualization; pneumothorax is the feared complication of any thoracic-level injection.

procedures.title: Lumbar Medial Branch / Facet Joint Block
procedures.target: Diagnostic block for lumbar facet-mediated pain and intra-articular facet injection.
procedures.position: Prone with a pillow under the abdomen; curvilinear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan: the facet joint appears as a hypoechoic gap between the superior and inferior articular processes; the medial branch target is the groove at the junction of the transverse process and the superior articular process. Paramedian sagittal scan shows the transverse processes as a trident pattern with the psoas deep and the facet column posteriorly.
procedures.technique: Needle in-plane from lateral to medial in the transverse view to the TP-SAP junction for the medial branch; for intra-articular injection, enter the hypoechoic joint cleft. After the needle is placed for a lumbar facet nerve block, the next step is to rotate the transducer to the long-axis view to localize the transverse process and confirm position (Greher et al., Anesthesiology 2004).
procedures.injectate: 0.3-0.5 mL per medial branch; 1-1.5 mL intra-articular.
procedures.pearls: Reported technical success for ultrasound-guided lumbar facet joint injection is 88-96 percent with fluoroscopic validation (Gofeld et al., Reg Anesth Pain Med 2012) - a favorite exam statistic.

procedures.title: Lumbar Selective Nerve Root Block
procedures.target: Diagnostic and therapeutic block for lumbosacral radicular pain.
procedures.position: Prone; curvilinear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Paramedian sagittal scan identifies the transverse processes; the exiting nerve root is found in the foramen between adjacent transverse processes, deep to the intertransverse ligament, dorsal to the psoas.
procedures.technique: Out-of-plane and in-plane approaches have been described; the needle is advanced from lateral to medial toward the dorsal aspect of the foramen, keeping the tip superficial to the spinal canal; Doppler is used to exclude the radicular artery (remember the artery of Adamkiewicz, usually left T9-L2).
procedures.pearls: Reported technical success is about 90 percent (Kim et al., Clin Orthop Surg 2013; Gofeld et al., Spine 2012). Nerve stimulation is not routinely required, and ultrasound does not increase intravascular injection rates compared with other image guidance in the published reports.

procedures.title: Subarachnoid (Intrathecal) Injection
procedures.target: Intrathecal access (for example drug-delivery trial or injection).
procedures.position: Prone or lateral; curvilinear transducer, paramedian sagittal approach.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Paramedian sagittal scan shows the laminae as a horse-head pattern; between laminae the ligamentum flavum-posterior dura complex appears as a hyperechoic line, with the anechoic CSF space and the hyperechoic anterior dura/posterior longitudinal ligament complex deeper; the cauda equina may be seen floating in CSF.
procedures.technique: Ultrasound is used mainly for pre-procedure scanning (level identification, depth to dura, midline and interlaminar window marking) with needle advancement by loss-of-resistance or under real-time paramedian in-plane guidance in expert hands.
procedures.pearls: The dural sac usually ends at S2; below this level intrathecal puncture is not possible. Anticoagulation status is critical for any neuraxial technique.

procedures.title: Caudal Epidural Injection
procedures.target: Epidural steroid injection for lumbosacral radicular pain; also entry point for caudal neurolysis.
procedures.position: Prone; high-frequency linear transducer (hockey-stick helpful).
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan at the sacral hiatus shows the two sacral cornua as hyperechoic mounds and the sacrococcygeal ligament as a hyperechoic band between them, with the hypoechoic hiatus beneath; longitudinal scan shows the hiatus and the floor of the sacral canal.
procedures.technique: In-plane longitudinal approach: a 22-25 G needle is advanced through the sacrococcygeal ligament into the sacral canal; advance only a short distance to stay below the dural sac; confirm with color Doppler during injection (flow into the canal) and watch for lack of subcutaneous swelling.
procedures.pearls: Failure to enter the canal, intravascular injection into the sacral venous plexus, and dural puncture are the main pitfalls; real-time Doppler confirmation of spread is a strong exam pearl.

procedures.title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection
procedures.target: Diagnostic and therapeutic injection for sacroiliac joint pain.
procedures.position: Prone; low-frequency curvilinear (or linear in slim patients).
procedures.sonoanatomy: Start transverse over the sacrum at the midline (median sacral crest), slide laterally to find the posterior superior iliac spine; the SI joint is the hypoechoic cleft between the sacrum medially and the ilium laterally; the lower (synovial) portion is the target.
procedures.technique: Out-of-plane (short-axis) or in-plane from medial to lateral into the inferior joint cleft, 1-2 cm above the most caudal extent; walk the needle off the ilium into the cleft.
procedures.pearls: Only the lower one-third of the joint is synovial and accessible; ultrasound reliably guides peri- and intra-articular lower-pole injection; correlate with provocative tests (FABER, Gaenslen, distraction, compression, thigh thrust) in the vignette.

procedures.title: Cervical Sympathetic Trunk (Stellate Ganglion) Block
procedures.target: Sympathetically mediated pain of the head, neck and upper limb (CRPS), vascular insufficiency, hot flashes.
procedures.position: Supine, neck slightly extended; high-frequency linear transducer at the C6 level.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Axial scan at C6 (Chassaignac tubercle): carotid artery medially, internal jugular vein anterolaterally, thyroid medially, longus colli muscle on the vertebral body; the sympathetic trunk lies in the prevertebral fascia over the longus colli. The ganglion itself sits anterior to the C7 transverse process and the neck of the first rib; the vertebral artery is unprotected (outside the foramen) at C7.
procedures.technique: In-plane lateral-to-medial approach to the surface of the longus colli under the prevertebral fascia, medial to the carotid sheath; Doppler to exclude the vertebral, carotid and inferior thyroidal vessels.
procedures.injectate: 3-5 mL local anesthetic (small volume, superficial to the muscle).
procedures.pearls: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) plus ipsilateral hand warming confirms success; risks include hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), hematoma, seizures from vertebral artery injection, and pneumothorax at low levels.

procedures.title: Suprascapular Nerve Block
procedures.target: Shoulder pain (often with supraspinatus/infraspinatus pathology), adhesive capsulitis, post-stroke shoulder pain.
procedures.position: Sitting or lateral, arm resting on the lap; high-frequency linear transducer in a coronal oblique plane over the supraspinous fossa.
procedures.sonoanatomy: The nerve runs through the suprascapular notch beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament; the suprascapular artery typically passes above the ligament - identify it with Doppler. The nerve then enters the spinoglenoid notch.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from medial (or lateral) into the floor of the supraspinous fossa at the notch; contact bone lightly then inject beside the nerve.
procedures.pearls: The suprascapular nerve innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus (classic exam question: infraspinatus is the listed muscle it supplies; subscapularis, teres minor and deltoid are not). Pneumothorax is possible if the needle slips anteriorly off the scapula.

procedures.title: Ilioinguinal / Iliohypogastric Nerve Block
procedures.target: Inguinal neuralgia, post-herniorrhaphy pain, lower abdominal wall pain.
procedures.position: Supine; high-frequency linear transducer near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
procedures.sonoanatomy: Three muscle layers are seen: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis; the nerves lie in the fascial plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, a few centimeters medial/cranial to the ASIS; the deep circumflex iliac artery runs close to the ilioinguinal nerve - check with Doppler.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from lateral to medial into the fascial plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis; hydrodissect the plane and bathe both nerves.
procedures.injectate: 5-10 mL local anesthetic +/- steroid shared in the plane.
procedures.pearls: Classic exam question: the artery lying close to the ilioinguinal nerve is a branch of the deep circumflex iliac artery. Too-deep injection enters the peritoneum; too-superficial injection misses the plane.

procedures.title: Greater Occipital Nerve Block
procedures.target: Occipital neuralgia, cervicogenic headache, migraine adjunct.
procedures.position: Sitting or prone with the neck flexed; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Distal target: at the superior nuchal line, the nerve lies medial to the occipital artery (find the artery with Doppler). Proximal target: at the C2 level the nerve crosses the obliquus capitis inferior muscle deep to the semispinalis capitis; identify the bifid C2 spinous process and slide laterally.
procedures.technique: In-plane or out-of-plane approach to the nerve at the chosen level; hydrodissect around it.
procedures.pearls: Using the occipital artery as the landmark reduces intravascular injection; proximal (C2) blocks target the nerve before muscular entrapment sites.

procedures.title: Median Nerve at the Wrist
procedures.target: Carpal tunnel syndrome - diagnosis, steroid injection, hydrodissection.
procedures.position: Supine or sitting, forearm supinated on the table; high-frequency linear transducer at the volar wrist crease.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan: the nerve is a honeycomb structure beneath the flexor retinaculum, between the flexor carpi radialis tendon radially and the palmaris longus/flexor digitorum superficialis tendons; tendons show anisotropy, nerves do not change much with toggling. Trace the nerve proximally in the forearm to confirm identity.
procedures.technique: In-plane ulnar-to-radial approach (keeps the needle away from the palmar cutaneous branch) into the carpal tunnel; for hydrodissection, inject to lift the retinaculum off the nerve and free the nerve from surrounding tissue.
procedures.injectate: 1-2 mL (steroid + local anesthetic) or 5 mL for hydrodissection (5 percent dextrose or saline).
procedures.pearls: Diagnostic criteria: cross-sectional area at the inlet of 10 mm2 or more is the common cut-off, plus flattening ratio, retinacular bowing, loss of fascicular pattern and hyperemia on Doppler; always compare with the contralateral side. The median nerve supplies opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and the first and second lumbricals - but not abductor pollicis longus (radial nerve); recurrent thenar branch injury is the key complication to avoid.

procedures.title: Ulnar Nerve at the Cubital Canal
procedures.target: Cubital tunnel syndrome - diagnosis and perineural injection.
procedures.position: Arm abducted and externally rotated, elbow flexed over a support; high-frequency linear transducer between the medial epicondyle and olecranon.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan behind the medial epicondyle: the nerve sits in the cubital canal under the arcuate (Osborne) ligament between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris; perform dynamic scanning during elbow flexion to detect subluxation or dislocation of the nerve over the epicondyle.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach to the nerve at the canal; inject perineurally, never into the fascicles (intraneural injection causes severe pain and damage).
procedures.pearls: Exam favorites: an accessory anconeus epitrochlearis muscle can compress the nerve in the canal; the ulnar nerve can be seen at Guyon canal at the wrist, between the axillary vessels in the arm, and on the anterior surface of the medial triceps head - but not at the lateral epicondyle.

procedures.title: Intercostal Nerve Block
procedures.target: Intercostal neuralgia, post-thoracotomy or post-herpetic pain, rib fracture pain.
procedures.position: Prone or lateral; high-frequency linear transducer in a parasagittal plane over the rib.
procedures.sonoanatomy: The rib is a hyperechoic convex line with shadowing; the pleura appears as a bright sliding line deep to the intercostal muscles; the nerve runs with the vein and artery at the inferior border of the rib (from above downward: vein, artery, nerve) between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from caudal to cranial to the inferior rib border; inject between internal and innermost intercostal muscle layers next to the neurovascular bundle, keeping the pleura in view at all times.
procedures.pearls: Pneumothorax is the principal complication - watch pleural sliding and keep the tip above the pleura; related fact: the most common complication of paravertebral block is vascular puncture (Naja et al., Anaesthesia 2001).

procedures.title: Saphenous Nerve Above the Knee
procedures.target: Saphenous neuralgia, knee surgery analgesia adjunct, medial leg pain.
procedures.position: Supine with the leg slightly externally rotated; high-frequency linear transducer over the medial distal thigh.
procedures.sonoanatomy: At the adductor (subsartorial) canal the nerve travels with the femoral artery under the sartorius; above the knee it is found between the sartorius and vastus medialis near the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery; distally it runs with the great saphenous vein.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from anterior to the nerve in the subsartorial plane above the knee; use Doppler to avoid genicular vessels.
procedures.pearls: The saphenous nerve is purely sensory below the knee (innervates medial leg and foot); a transsartorial approach is an alternative at knee level.

procedures.title: Tibial Nerve at the Tarsal Canal
procedures.target: Tarsal tunnel syndrome - diagnosis and perineural injection.
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus or supine with the hip externally rotated; high- frequency linear transducer behind the medial malleolus.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan posterior to the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, remembering the order from anterior to posterior: tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial artery and veins, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus tendon (mnemonic Tom, Dick ANd Harry). The nerve appears honeycombed beside the pulsatile artery (Doppler).
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from posterior or anterior into the tunnel beside the nerve; hydrodissect if adhesions are suspected.
procedures.pearls: Assess for space-occupying causes (ganglia, tenosynovitis, varicosities) and measure nerve cross-section; avoid intraneural injection.

procedures.title: Pudendal Nerve Block
procedures.target: Pudendal neuralgia (perineal pain worse with sitting).
procedures.position: Prone; low-frequency curvilinear transducer in a transverse oblique plane at the level of the ischial spine.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Identify the ischial spine as a hyperechoic peak; the sacrospinous ligament attaches to it medially and the sacrotuberous ligament lies superficial/medial; the pudendal nerve lies in the interligamentous plane medial to the ischial spine, beside the internal pudendal artery (confirm with Doppler).
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from medial to lateral into the interligamentous space beside the artery; hydrodissect the plane.
procedures.pearls: Exam favorites: the nerve is readily found medial to the ischial spine; electrical stimulation of the pudendal nerve activates the levator ani and coccygeus. Vaginal or rectal wall puncture and intravascular injection are the main risks.

procedures.title: Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Block
procedures.target: Meralgia paresthetica (anterolateral thigh burning/numbness).
procedures.position: Supine; high-frequency linear transducer starting at the ASIS, sliding medially and distally.
procedures.sonoanatomy: The nerve is classically a small hyperechoic dot with a hypoechoic rim (the cat-eye appearance) lying over the sartorius muscle beneath the fascia lata, medial and caudal to the ASIS; anatomy is highly variable - scan between sartorius and tensor fascia lata and trace proximally toward the inguinal ligament.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from lateral to medial to the nerve; hydrodissect beneath the fascia lata where entrapment occurs.
procedures.pearls: Classic exam question: the classic appearance is the cat eye with a hyperechoic center over the sartorius; negative block does not exclude the diagnosis because of anatomical variability - scan both sides for comparison.

procedures.title: Acromioclavicular Joint Injection
procedures.target: AC joint arthrosis or post-traumatic AC joint pain (the sample oral case).
procedures.position: Sitting, arm resting at the side; high-frequency linear transducer over the apex of the joint (clavicle-acromion line).
procedures.sonoanatomy: The joint is the hypoechoic gap between the hyperechoic distal clavicle and acromion, capped by the hyperechoic AC ligament; measure the acromion-clavicle distance and compare with the other side; dynamic cross-body adduction widens/narrows the gap and reproduces pain.
procedures.technique: Out-of-plane or in-plane approach (use a gel step-off for the in-plane approach on small joints); a 25 G needle is placed under the AC ligament into the joint cleft; watch the fluid distend the joint.
procedures.injectate: 1-2 mL (20-40 mg triamcinolone or 3-6 mg betamethasone in lidocaine).
procedures.pearls: Complications to quote: infection, hyperglycemia, skin discoloration, pain flare, tendon rupture (regional), and pneumothorax (deep medial needle). Conservative care first for Rockwood type I-III injuries; types IV-VI usually need surgery.

procedures.title: Biceps Tendon (Peritendinous) Injection
procedures.target: Biceps tendinopathy or tenosynovitis of the long head of biceps.
procedures.position: Supine or sitting, arm on the lap in neutral or slight external rotation; high-frequency linear transducer over the anterior shoulder.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan shows the bicipital groove between the greater and lesser tuberosities, roofed by the transverse humeral ligament; the tendon is oval and fibrillar - toggle to control anisotropy; a branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery runs in the groove (Doppler); the subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from lateral into the tendon sheath (peritendinous), never into the tendon substance; confirm spread around the tendon in short axis.
procedures.injectate: 2-3 mL steroid + local anesthetic into the sheath.
procedures.pearls: Intratendinous steroid risks rupture; evaluate for associated pulley lesions and subluxation with dynamic internal/external rotation.

procedures.title: Glenohumeral Joint Injection
procedures.target: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis, adhesive capsulitis (with distension), inflammatory arthritis.
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus or sitting with the arm across the chest; the posterior approach is standard with a linear or curvilinear transducer over the posterior shoulder.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Posterior transverse scan shows the infraspinatus tendon over the humeral head, the glenoid and the posterior labrum; gentle external rotation opens the posterior recess and helps identify the joint line.
procedures.technique: In-plane lateral-to-medial approach: the needle passes through infraspinatus into the posterior recess between humeral head and glenoid labrum; confirm intra- articular spread in real time.
procedures.injectate: 4-5 mL steroid + local anesthetic (up to 20-30 mL for hydrodistension in capsulitis).
procedures.pearls: Avoid the labrum; the anterior approach via the rotator interval is an alternative; suprascapular nerve block is the related exam target.

procedures.title: Subdeltoid Bursa Injection
procedures.target: Subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis, impingement-related shoulder pain.
procedures.position: Sitting with the hand on the ipsilateral hip (modified Crass) or arm in extension/internal rotation to expose the supraspinatus; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Long-axis view of the supraspinatus: the bursa is the thin hypoechoic line between the deltoid above and the supraspinatus tendon below, extending under the acromion; distended bursa shows fluid and sometimes synovial thickening.
procedures.technique: In-plane lateral-to-medial approach along the supraspinatus long axis, sliding the needle over the tendon into the bursal space; inject under direct vision - the bursa should separate and fill.
procedures.pearls: Do not inject the supraspinatus tendon itself (resistance and beading mean you are intratendinous); check for impingement dynamically with abduction.

procedures.title: Elbow Joint Injection
procedures.target: Elbow osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, joint effusion.
procedures.position: Supine or sitting, elbow flexed 90 degrees across the abdomen; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Posterior approach: longitudinal scan over the triceps shows the olecranon fossa; effusion lifts the posterior fat pad. Lateral approach: transverse over the radiocapitellar joint shows the radial head rotating with pronation/supination and the annular recess.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach into the olecranon fossa from lateral, or into the radiocapitellar joint from posterolateral; confirm spread in the recess.
procedures.pearls: Keep away from the radial nerve (anterior) and the ulnar nerve (posteromedial in the cubital canal); aspiration first if effusion is present.

procedures.title: Epicondylosis: Tendon Sheath Injection / Fenestration
procedures.target: Lateral or medial epicondylosis refractory to conservative care.
procedures.position: Sitting, elbow flexed and supported, forearm pronated for the lateral side; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Long-axis scan of the common extensor tendon at the lateral epicondyle (or common flexor tendon medially): tendinosis appears as hypoechoic thickening with loss of fibrillar pattern, possible calcification, cortical irregularity and hyperemia on power Doppler; compare with the other side.
procedures.technique: Peritendinous injection around the tendon origin, or dry-needle fenestration (peppering): multiple passes through the diseased tendon with a 22-25 G needle to induce bleeding and healing response; PRP or prolotherapy are described alternatives.
procedures.injectate: 1-2 mL around the tendon; fenestration without steroid or with autologous product.
procedures.pearls: Avoid repeated intratendinous steroid (collagen weakening, rupture); respect the radial nerve/posterior interosseous nerve anteriorly and the ulnar collateral ligament medially.

procedures.title: First Metacarpophalangeal Joint Injection
procedures.target: First MCP (thumb) osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis.
procedures.position: Hand resting palm-down or neutral on the table; high-frequency linear or hockey-stick transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Dorsal longitudinal scan shows the metacarpal head and proximal phalanx base with the hypoechoic joint recess; the extensor pollicis brevis tendon crosses dorsally; sesamoids lie volar.
procedures.technique: In-plane distal-to-proximal (or out-of-plane) approach into the dorsal recess with a 25-30 G needle; traction on the thumb can open the joint.
procedures.pearls: Small joint - use small volumes; avoid the extensor tendon and radial sensory branches; ultrasound improves accuracy in small joints versus landmark technique.

procedures.title: Piriformis Injection
procedures.target: Piriformis syndrome (buttock pain with sciatica without radiculopathy).
procedures.position: Prone; low-frequency curvilinear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse oblique scan at the level of the sciatic notch: identify the lateral border of the sacrum medially and the ilium laterally; the piriformis stretches between them deep to the gluteus maximus; the sciatic nerve lies lateral/deep to the muscle at the infrapiriform fossa and must be identified before needling.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from medial to lateral into the muscle belly; confirm position with a small test injection (hydro-location) and watch the muscle expand.
procedures.injectate: 3-5 mL local anesthetic +/- steroid (or botulinum toxin in specialist practice).
procedures.pearls: Watch the sciatic nerve, the inferior gluteal artery (Doppler) and the pudendal structures medially; reproduction of concordant buttock pain on palpation/scanning supports the diagnosis.

procedures.title: Hip Joint Injection
procedures.target: Hip osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, diagnostic block before further treatment.
procedures.position: Supine with the leg in neutral or slight internal rotation; low- frequency curvilinear transducer over the anterior hip (linear in slim patients).
procedures.sonoanatomy: Longitudinal scan along the femoral neck: the hyperechoic line of the femoral head-neck junction, the acetabular rim and labrum cranially, the anterior synovial recess draped over the neck under the iliofemoral ligament; the psoas tendon and femoral neurovascular bundle lie medially - map with Doppler.
procedures.technique: In-plane lateral-to-medial (or caudal-to-cranial) approach along the femoral neck into the anterior recess; confirm capsular distension with injection.
procedures.pearls: Keep lateral to the femoral vessels; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve crosses superficially - do not spear it; the anterior recess is shallow, so small test injections help confirm the space.

procedures.title: Trochanteric Bursa Complex Injection
procedures.target: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (bursitis, gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy).
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus, painful side up; high-frequency linear or curvilinear transducer over the greater trochanter.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Transverse scan over the lateral facet of the greater trochanter: the gluteus medius inserts on the lateral/posterior facets and the gluteus minimus on the anterior facet, covered by the iliotibial band/gluteus maximus; the subgluteus maximus (trochanteric) bursa lies between the ITB and the gluteus medius tendon; distension or tendon hypoechogenicity may be seen.
procedures.technique: In-plane anterior-to-posterior approach into the bursa between the ITB and the gluteus medius tendon; observe bursal filling rather than tendon injection.
procedures.pearls: GTPS is more often tendinopathy than pure bursitis - describe tendon findings in the oral exam; compare sides and use Doppler for hyperemia.

procedures.title: Knee Joint Injection
procedures.target: Knee osteoarthritis, effusion, inflammatory arthritis.
procedures.position: Supine, knee slightly flexed on a roll; high-frequency linear transducer.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Suprapatellar approach: longitudinal scan over the quadriceps tendon shows the suprapatellar pouch between the prefemoral and suprapatellar fat pads; effusion collects here first. Medial/lateral parapatellar recesses are alternatives; the cartilage over the femoral condyles is anechoic.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from lateral (or medial) into the suprapatellar pouch or the parapatellar recess; aspirate effusion first if present, then inject without resistance.
procedures.injectate: 5-10 mL steroid + local anesthetic (viscosupplement as an alternative).
procedures.pearls: The superolateral approach has the highest accuracy; confirm intra- articular flow in real time; examine the medial meniscus extrusion, collateral ligaments and Baker cyst as part of the regional overview in the oral exam.

procedures.title: Distal Iliotibial Band Peritendon Injection
procedures.target: Iliotibial band syndrome (lateral knee pain in runners/cyclists).
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus or supine with the knee flexed about 30 degrees; high-frequency linear transducer over the lateral femoral epicondyle.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Longitudinal and transverse scans show the ITB as a fibrillar band gliding over the lateral femoral epicondyle; pathology shows peritendinous fluid or thickening between the band and the epicondyle; dynamic flexion/extension may demonstrate snapping.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach to the plane between the ITB and the lateral epicondyle; inject peritendinously, not into the band.
procedures.pearls: Differentiate from lateral meniscus and lateral collateral ligament pathology on examination; anisotropy can mimic thickening - toggle the probe.

procedures.title: Tibiotalar Joint Injection
procedures.target: Ankle osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, effusion.
procedures.position: Supine with the foot plantigrade on the table; high-frequency linear transducer over the anterior ankle.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Longitudinal scan shows the distal tibia and the talar neck with the anterior recess between them; effusion distends the recess; the tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus tendons cross dorsally and the dorsalis pedis artery lies lateral to the EHL - map with Doppler.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from distal to proximal (or out-of-plane) into the anterior recess, avoiding the neurovascular bundle; small 25 G needle.
procedures.pearls: The dorsalis pedis artery is the structure to avoid; plantarflexion opens the recess; aspiration before injection if septic arthritis is a consideration.

procedures.title: Subtalar Joint Injection
procedures.target: Subtalar (posterior facet) arthritis, post-calcaneal fracture pain.
procedures.position: Lateral decubitus with the lateral side up, or supine with inversion; high-frequency linear transducer at the sinus tarsi.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Scan obliquely over the sinus tarsi between the talus and calcaneus; the posterior facet joint is the hypoechoic gap deeper and posterior; the peroneal tendons run superficially in the lateral hindfoot and must be avoided.
procedures.technique: In-plane approach from anterolateral (sinus tarsi) into the posterior facet cleft; small 25 G needle; confirm with a test injection.
procedures.pearls: Small, curved joint - only the posterior facet is injected; reproduce concordant pain with hindfoot inversion/eversion on examination in the vignette.

procedures.title: First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Injection
procedures.target: First MTP osteoarthritis (hallux rigidus), gout, sesamoid-region pain.
procedures.position: Supine with the foot flat; high-frequency linear or hockey-stick transducer over the dorsum of the joint.
procedures.sonoanatomy: Dorsal longitudinal scan shows the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx base, dorsal osteophytes in hallux rigidus, and the joint recess; the extensor hallucis longus tendon crosses dorsally; tophaceous gout shows hyperechoic aggregates and a double-contour sign over cartilage.
procedures.technique: In-plane distal-to-proximal approach into the dorsal recess with a 25 G needle; gentle toe traction opens the space.
procedures.pearls: Small volume only; avoid the EHL tendon and dorsalis pedis branches; the double-contour sign is a classic gout finding to quote.

weeks.title: Orientation, Physics and Knobology
weeks.read: NAR 1-4 (imaging, pitfalls, knobology, needle visibility); PEN 1 (physics); BIG 5-6 and 10 (equipment, sonography principles, needle technology); JAC 1 (instrumentation).
weeks.scan: Daily 15-minute knobology drills on any volunteer - depth, gain, TGC, focus, frequency, compound imaging, beam steering, color and power Doppler; practice entering patient data and saving labeled images (documentation standards).

weeks.title: Cervical Spine
weeks.read: NAR 5-8 (spine sonoanatomy, third occipital nerve and cervical medial branch, cervical facet, cervical nerve root); PEN 12-13; KAR 5-6 (spine basics, cervical spine); JAN 15 (cervical medial branch and RFA); RAPM Part II (cervical sections).
weeks.scan: Articular pillar sawtooth and pillar waist; two-humped camel transverse processes; level counting from C2 and C7; vertebral artery on Doppler at every level.
weeks.test: Explain aloud why the needle tip must stay on bone at the pillar waist.

weeks.title: Thoracolumbar Spine and Sacroiliac Joint
weeks.read: NAR 9-14 (thoracic paravertebral, lumbar facet, lumbar nerve root, central neuraxial, caudal, SI joint); PEN 14-17 (lumbar medial branches and L5 dorsal ramus, SI joint and lateral branches, SIJ radiofrequency, caudal); KAR 7-9 and 11; BIG 36-38 and 50; KOR practice points on axial injections.
weeks.scan: Lumbar trident and horse-head windows; sacral hiatus between cornua; SI joint cleft at the lower pole; measure depth to the lamina on a volunteer.

weeks.title: Autonomic and Head/Neck Nerves
weeks.read: PEN 2-3 (occipital nerves, cervical sympathetic trunk); NAR 22-24 and 31; JAN 11-12 (occipital block, cervical sympathetic chain); BIG 44-45 (stellate); RAPM Part I (stellate ganglion).
weeks.scan: C6 anterior tubercle, longus colli and carotid sheath; locate the occipital artery with Doppler and find the greater occipital nerve medial to it.
weeks.test: Name six structures to avoid at C6 and the sign of a successful stellate block.

weeks.title: Trunk and Abdominal Wall Nerves
weeks.read: PEN 5-7 and 11 (intercostal, ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric, genitofemoral, erector spinae plane); BIG 34-37; KAR 4 and 10; WAL 92 and 100-102.
weeks.scan: Rib-pleura interface with breathing; the vein-artery-nerve order at the inferior rib border; three muscle layers near the ASIS and the deep circumflex iliac artery on Doppler.
weeks.test: MCQ Bank Volume 2, Section D questions on trunk nerves.

weeks.title: Pelvic and Lower-Limb Nerves
weeks.read: PEN 8-10 (pelvic muscles, pudendal and inferior cluneal, LFCN); BIG 24-25 and 49; RAPM Part I (LFCN, pudendal, piriformis sections).
weeks.scan: LFCN over the sartorius (cat-eye) with side comparison; ischial spine and interligamentous plane with internal pudendal artery on Doppler; saphenous nerve in the subsartorial canal.

weeks.title: Shoulder and Elbow
weeks.read: JAC 3-4 (the core diagnostic chapters); PEN 19-20; NAR 26-27; RAPM Part III (shoulder); WAL 35-62 for any technique you have not seen.
weeks.scan: Complete shoulder protocol - biceps groove, subscapularis, supraspinatus in Crass and modified Crass, AC joint with cross-body adduction, posterior recess; elbow - anterior recess, radiocapitellar joint, common extensor origin, cubital canal with dynamic flexion.
weeks.test: Perform the shoulder ultrasound examination aloud in 10 minutes against the 12-item checklist.

weeks.title: Wrist, Hand and Diagnostic Nerve Ultrasound
weeks.read: JAC 5; PEN 21; NAR 30 (ultrasonography of peripheral nerves); WAL 63-81; BIG 13 (intraneural injection - the human data).
weeks.scan: Median nerve CSA at the inlet on both sides and calculate the wrist-to-forearm ratio; ulnar nerve at Guyon canal; trace nerves proximally to confirm identity (the elevator technique).
weeks.test: MCQ Bank Volume 2, Section E questions on upper limb.

weeks.title: Hip and Knee
weeks.read: JAC 6-7; PEN 22-23; NAR 28-29; RAPM Part IV (hip) and Part V (knee); PEN 27 (hip and knee denervation) for oral-exam depth.
weeks.scan: Femoral neck long axis and anterior recess; trochanter facets with gluteus medius/minimus insertions; suprapatellar pouch, cartilage in full flexion, medial meniscus extrusion, Baker cyst corner.

weeks.read: JAC 8; PEN 24-26 (ankle, PRP, calcific tendinitis intervention); RAPM Part VI (ankle); WAL 154-179 as needed.

weeks.read: JAN 4-5 (serious complications, local anesthetic systemic toxicity); FIPP pharmacology and radiofrequency chapters for theory gaps; KOR cover to cover; PEN 16 (SIJ radiofrequency) and the anticoagulation guidance in your procedure chapters.
weeks.scan: None new - consolidate; build your personal complication list for every one of the 20 practical procedures.

weeks.read: Re-read the examiner checklists in the Study Guide; skim KOR practice points daily.
