cases.title: Meralgia Paresthetica
cases.vignette: A 45-year-old overweight man presents with a 6-month history of burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh. Symptoms are worse after prolonged standing and walking and are relieved by sitting. He recently gained weight and wears a tight tool belt at work. He denies back pain, weakness, or sphincter symptoms. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) entrapment (meralgia paresthetica) - most likely; L2 or L3 lumbar radiculopathy; lumbar plexopathy; femoral neuropathy; hip joint pathology with referred pain; diabetic mononeuropathy. Key differentiators: meralgia paresthetica is purely sensory, spares motor function and reflexes, and does not cross the midline or extend below the knee.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting, then standing. Inspection for asymmetry or skin changes. Sensory examination with tools: pinprick (toothpick) and light touch (brush) mapped over the anterolateral thigh and compared with the other side; vibration (tuning fork) at the malleoli for a peripheral neuropathy screen. Tinel sign over the LFCN medial to the ASIS. Neurological examination with reflex hammer: patellar reflexes, hip flexion and knee extension power - all expected normal. Hip range of motion and lumbar screen to exclude referred pain. Pelvic compression test (side-lying, downward pressure on the pelvis) - relief supports LFCN entrapment under the inguinal ligament.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: The diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound localizes the nerve and compares sides. Order fasting glucose/HbA1c (diabetes predisposes). Nerve conduction studies if the picture is atypical. Lumbar spine MRI only if radicular features appear. Weight and metabolic risk assessment.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Enter patient information, clean the probe, wear gloves, place the machine ergonomically. Regional overview of the inguinal region from the ASIS. Find the nerve in short axis: a small cat-eye structure over the sartorius beneath the fascia lata, medial and caudal to the ASIS; trace it proximally toward the inguinal ligament. Compare cross- section and echogenicity with the contralateral side (the affected nerve may be swollen and hypoechoic). Apply color Doppler to map accompanying vessels. Name on request: sartorius, tensor fascia lata, fascia lata, ASIS, inguinal ligament, the nerve itself.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Remove the entrapment source: weight loss, loose clothing, repositioning the tool belt. Topical lidocaine or capsaicin for focal symptoms. Neuropathic agents (gabapentin or pregabalin; duloxetine or a tricyclic as alternatives). NSAIDs short term. Activity modification.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided LFCN perineural block with local anesthetic and corticosteroid, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Persistent cases may be considered for pulsed radiofrequency of the LFCN; surgery (neurolysis) is a last resort.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Supine position; high-frequency linear transducer. Identify the nerve over the sartorius under the fascia lata medial/caudal to the ASIS; confirm with Doppler that no vessel shares the path. Prep skin, sterile gel, gloves, probe cover. In-plane lateral-to-medial approach with a 25 G needle to the perineural plane; hydrodissect beneath the fascia lata with 3-5 mL total, for example 0.25% bupivacaine with 20-40 mg triamcinolone. Observe spread around the nerve in real time.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Intraneural injection with nerve injury (stop if the patient reports severe paresthesia); intravascular injection; hematoma; infection; transient worsened numbness; steroid- related skin depigmentation and fat atrophy; block failure owing to the nerve's anatomical variability - scan both sides and trace the nerve if it is not found at the classic site.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Map pain relief against the block duration (diagnostic value); repeat the sensory examination; assess walking tolerance and sleep; reinforce weight and belt modification; record response to plan repeat injection or pulsed radiofrequency if relief is significant but temporary.

cases.title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
cases.vignette: A 52-year-old woman with hypothyroidism describes 8 months of numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers of the right hand. Symptoms wake her at night, and shaking the hand gives relief. She drops objects. She works at a computer. There is no neck pain. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve entrapment at the wrist) - most likely; C6 or C7 cervical radiculopathy; proximal median neuropathy (pronator teres syndrome); peripheral polyneuropathy; de Quervain tenosynovitis or thumb CMC arthritis if pain predominates. Night symptoms, the flick sign and median distribution favor CTS.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting with both hands accessible. Inspection for thenar atrophy. Sensory examination with tools: pinprick (toothpick) and light touch (brush) comparing median and ulnar digits, and the thenar eminence (palmar cutaneous branch is spared in CTS); two-point discrimination if available. Provocative tests: Phalen maneuver, Tinel over the carpal tunnel, Durkan carpal compression test. Motor: abductor pollicis brevis strength against resistance. Reflex hammer: biceps, brachioradialis, triceps. Cervical screen with range of motion and Spurling test to exclude radiculopathy.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Ultrasound measurement of the median nerve cross-sectional area (first-line and immediately available at the bedside). Nerve conduction studies/EMG to grade severity or when surgery is contemplated. Thyroid function and glucose to address contributing causes.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview of the volar wrist in short axis; then focus on the tunnel inlet at the pisiform level. Measure the median nerve cross-sectional area (ellipse or trace method) - 10 mm2 or more supports CTS; compare with the contralateral side and note a wrist- to-forearm ratio. Assess retinacular bowing, flattening ratio, loss of fascicular pattern, and hyperemia with power Doppler. Dynamic examination: finger flexion to watch tendon and nerve gliding. Name on request: flexor retinaculum, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum tendons, median nerve, ulnar artery and nerve at Guyon canal.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Neutral-position night wrist splinting; activity and ergonomic modification; treat hypothyroidism; NSAIDs for symptomatic relief; a trial of ultrasound-guided steroid injection is both diagnostic and therapeutic and oken follows failed splinting.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided carpal tunnel corticosteroid injection. An evidence-based alternative is hydrodissection of the median nerve with 5% dextrose to free it from perineural adhesions.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Forearm supinated on a support; high-frequency linear transducer in short axis over the tunnel. In-plane ulnar-to-radial approach with a 25 G needle, entering from the ulnar side to stay clear of the palmar cutaneous and recurrent thenar branches; slide the tip between the retinaculum and the nerve. Inject 1-2 mL (for example betamethasone 3-6 mg in lidocaine) and watch the retinaculum lik; for hydrodissection use about 5 mL of 5% dextrose to circumferentially free the nerve. Confirm no intravascular flow on Doppler beforehand.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Intraneural injection (median nerve injury); injury to the recurrent thenar motor branch or the palmar cutaneous branch; vascular puncture (ulnar artery); infection; post- injection flare; skin depigmentation; tendon weakening with repeated exposure; transient worsening of paresthesias.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Night symptom relief usually comes first - quantify it; re-test Tinel and Phalen and abductor pollicis brevis strength; document duration of response to guide repeat injection versus surgical decompression; repeat the cross-sectional area measurement on follow-up; ensure thyroid and glycemic management continues.

cases.title: Cervical Facet Pain after Whiplash
cases.vignette: A 48-year-old man presents with persistent right-sided neck pain and right occipital headache 12 months after a rear-end motor vehicle collision. Pain is worse with extension and rotation to the right. There is no arm pain or numbness. Ibuprofen and physiotherapy gave partial relief. Neurological examination has been normal. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Cervical facet (zygapophysial) joint syndrome, typically C2-3 (third occipital nerve) or C3-4 aker whiplash - most likely; cervical radiculopathy; discogenic pain; myofascial pain; greater occipital neuralgia; cervicogenic headache from other upper cervical sources.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting. Cervical active and passive range of motion in all planes - extension with ipsilateral rotation (facet loading/Kemp maneuver) should reproduce concordant pain. Palpation over the articular pillars and occipital ridge. Neurological examination with tools: biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes with the hammer; dermatomal sensation with toothpick and brush; upper-limb power and tone; Spurling test negative. Tinel over the greater occipital nerve. Shoulder screen to exclude referred shoulder pathology.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Plain radiographs or MRI to exclude fracture, instability or disc pathology (usually unremarkable in facet syndrome); imaging cannot confirm the pain generator. The definitive diagnostic test is a controlled (comparative local anesthetic or placebo- controlled) medial branch block of the suspected levels.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview of the lateral cervical spine with the model in lateral decubitus or sitting. Count levels from the bifid C2 spinous process. Identify the sawtooth line of the articular pillars in the axial plane and the groove (waist) of the pillar at the target level, where the medial branch sits. Compare both sides. Color Doppler along the planned needle path - the vertebral artery runs anteriorly at foraminal level. Name on request: articular pillars, facet joint gaps, transverse processes, sternocleidomastoid, levator scapulae, vertebral artery.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Structured physiotherapy (posture re-education, deep neck flexor and scapular strengthening), manual therapy, NSAIDs, TENS, activity modification, and addressing any post-traumatic stress component - before escalating to interventional diagnosis and treatment.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided cervical medial branch blocks at the appropriate levels (each joint has dual innervation, so two levels per joint) as a diagnostic and prognostic procedure; aker a concordant positive response, medial branch radiofrequency neurotomy is the definitive treatment.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Lateral decubitus, symptomatic side up; high-frequency linear transducer. Axial view: identify the sawtooth pillars and the target waist. Doppler for vessels. In-plane approach from posterior/lateral with a 25 G needle to the waist of the articular pillar until the tip rests on bone; confirm in two planes. Inject 0.3-0.5 mL of local anesthetic per level (for a purely diagnostic block), observing spread and keeping the tip on bone throughout.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Vertebral artery injection (seizure) - prevented by Doppler and keeping the tip on bone; unintended nerve root or epidural spread causing transient arm numbness/weakness; ataxia or dizziness from loss of proprioceptive input; hematoma; infection; vasovagal reaction. For later radiofrequency add neuritis and post-procedure soreness.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Pain diary during the expected anesthetic duration - concordant relief (commonly 80% or more) constitutes a positive diagnostic block; document range-of-motion change; schedule the comparative second block; if positive, proceed to radiofrequency neurotomy and review at 4-8 weeks for neuritis and functional gain.

cases.title: Lumbosacral Radicular Pain
cases.vignette: A 55-year-old man describes 4 months of right leg pain radiating from the buPock to the dorsum of the foot after lifting a heavy box. Pain is worse with sitting and coughing, with tingling in the same distribution. MRI shows a right posterolateral L4-5 disc herniation. NSAIDs and 6 weeks of physiotherapy have not controlled the pain. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Right L5 radiculopathy from the L4-5 disc herniation - most likely (a posterolateral herniation at L4-5 typically affects the traversing L5 root); lumbar facet syndrome; sacroiliac joint pain; piriformis syndrome; lumbar spinal stenosis. Dermatomal radiation below the knee with cough impulse favors radiculopathy.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Observe gait and standing posture (antalgic list). Lumbar active and passive range of motion. Straight leg raise (Lasègue) and slump test - reproduction of leg pain between 30-70 degrees supports root tension. Neurological examination with tools: patellar and Achilles reflexes with the hammer; great toe dorsiflexion (EHL, L5), foot dorsiflexion (L4- L5) and plantarflexion (S1) power; sensation with toothpick and brush over the L4, L5 and S1 dermatomes; tone. Screen for red flags: saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction - absent here.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: MRI is already available and correlates with the examination - ensure the level and side match the clinical findings before intervening. No further imaging is routinely needed; EMG/NCS only if the diagnosis is in doubt or deficit is chronic. Baseline coagulation status and medication review before injection.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview with a curvilinear transducer in the paramedian sagittal plane, counting levels from the sacrum. Identify the trident pattern of the lumbar transverse processes and the interlaminar windows (horse-head laminae). Focus on the foramen between the L5 transverse process and the sacrum for the exiting L5 root (or L4-5 foramen as indicated): the root is seen dorsal to the psoas between adjacent transverse processes. Color Doppler along the planned path to exclude radicular vessels - remember the artery of Adamkiewicz (usually lek T9-L2). Name on request: transverse processes, facet column, psoas, the exiting root.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Continue structured physiotherapy with directional-preference exercises; neuropathic pain agents (gabapentinoid or SNRI) for the radicular component; NSAIDs short term; activity modification with avoidance of provocative liking; education on the favorable natural history of disc herniation.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided selective nerve root block (transforaminal epidural) of the affected root - reported technical success is about 90% in the literature; it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Caudal epidural injection is the alternative ultrasound-guided route for multilevel or post-surgical pain.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Prone position; curvilinear transducer. Paramedian sagittal scan to count levels and locate the foramen; rotate to optimize the root view. Doppler to exclude the radicular artery. In-plane needle approach from lateral to medial with a 22-25 G needle toward the dorsal aspect of the foramen, keeping the tip superficial to the canal and visualized at all times; stop for any paresthesia. Aker negative aspiration inject 1-2 mL slowly (for example lidocaine with betamethasone 3-6 mg), watching real-time spread without vascular runoff.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Intravascular injection into a radicular artery with risk of spinal cord infarction - the reason for Doppler, dorsal needle position and real-time observation of injectate; direct nerve injury; transient paresthesia or weakness; dural puncture if the needle advances too deep; infection; steroid side effects (hyperglycemia, flare).

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Immediate post-procedure neurological check (power, sensation) before discharge; concordance and duration of leg-pain relief for the diagnostic value; function (sitting tolerance, walking distance); plan repeat injection or surgical consultation if a fixed neurological deficit or refractory pain persists; reinforce the rehabilitation program.

cases.title: Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome
cases.vignette: A 60-year-old woman presents with 7 months of right lateral hip pain. It is worse when she lies on the right side and when climbing stairs. She points with one finger to the greater trochanter. There is no back pain and no groin pain. Paracetamol helps liPle. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy with trochanteric bursal involvement) - most likely; hip osteoarthritis (groin-predominant, restricted rotation); lumbar referred pain (L2-L4); meralgia paresthetica (purely sensory); iliotibial band pathology; rarely, gluteus medius tear or avulsion.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Observe gait for a Trendelenburg pattern and test single-leg stance. Position the model side-lying with the painful side up. Palpate the greater trochanter facets for point tenderness. Resisted hip abduction - pain and weakness support gluteus medius tendinopathy. Hip active and passive range of motion (internal rotation preserved argues against OA). FABER (Patrick) test. Lumbar screen and neurological examination with reflex hammer (patellar reflexes) and sensory mapping with brush to exclude radicular referral.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Ultrasound of the trochanteric region is first-line and immediately available. Pelvic radiograph if hip OA is suspected or the diagnosis is unclear. MRI only for suspected tendon tear or failed treatment. No routine laboratory testing.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview in lateral decubitus: transverse scan over the greater trochanter to display the anterior, lateral and posterior facets. Focus on the insertions: gluteus minimus on the anterior facet, gluteus medius on the lateral and posterior facets, with the iliotibial band and gluteus maximus superficial. Look for tendon thickening, hypoechogenicity, cortical irregularity, calcification, tears, and fluid in the subgluteus maximus bursa between the ITB and the gluteus medius tendon. Power Doppler for hyperemia. Measure tendon thickness and compare with the contralateral side. Name on request: greater trochanter facets, gluteus medius and minimus tendons, ITB, bursa.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Load management and physiotherapy focused on hip abductor strengthening and ITB/gluteal flexibility; avoid lying on the painful side and prolonged crossed-leg sitting; weight loss; NSAIDs topical or oral; TENS. Most cases improve with exercise-based care before injection is needed.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided subgluteus maximus (trochanteric) bursa corticosteroid injection. For predominant tendinopathy refractory to injection, PRP injection into the gluteus medius tendon may be considered.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Lateral decubitus, symptomatic side up; linear or curvilinear transducer depending on habitus. Identify the bursal plane between the iliotibial band and the gluteus medius tendon at the lateral facet; Doppler for vessels. In-plane anterior-to-posterior approach with a 22-25 G needle into the bursa; inject 3-5 mL (for example triamcinolone 40 mg in 0.25% bupivacaine) and watch the bursa distend without resistance. If the tendon itself is treated (PRP), fenestrate the diseased fibers under direct vision instead of injecting steroid into the tendon.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Infection; post-injection flare; skin depigmentation and fat atrophy from too-superficial steroid placement; tendon weakening with repeated intratendinous steroid; intravascular injection; vasovagal reaction; transient increased pain.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Night pain and side-lying tolerance; point tenderness on re-palpation; abductor strength and Trendelenburg sign; stair function; emphasize that injection is a window for the strengthening program, and review at 4-6 weeks to decide on repeat injection, PRP, or further imaging if the response is poor.

cases.title: Knee Osteoarthritis with Effusion
cases.vignette: A 68-year-old overweight man reports 2 years of progressive right knee pain with less than 30 minutes of morning stiffness, pain on stairs, and intermiPent swelling. Weight-bearing radiographs show medial compartment joint-space narrowing with osteophytes. He asks for something to help him stay active. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Medial compartment knee osteoarthritis with effusion - most likely; degenerative medial meniscus tear; inflammatory arthritis (less likely with short morning stiffness); pes anserine bursitis (medial below the joint line); Baker cyst; referred pain from the hip.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Observe gait for a varus thrust. Position the model supine and then sitting. Compare circumference of both knees. Test active and passive range of motion and note crepitus. Assess effusion with the sweep (bulge) test and patellar ballottement. Palpate the medial joint line. Check ligament stability and neurovascular status; examine the ipsilateral hip to exclude referred pain. Neurological screen with patellar reflexes using the hammer.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Weight-bearing radiographs are already diagnostic. Ultrasound now to quantify the effusion, assess cartilage, look for medial meniscus extrusion and a Baker cyst, and to guide aspiration/injection. Joint fluid analysis only if infection or crystal disease is suspected; inflammatory markers if systemic disease is suspected.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview supine with the knee slightly flexed: longitudinal suprapatellar scan to measure the suprapatellar pouch between the prefemoral and suprapatellar fat pads; compare with the other side. Assess cartilage over the femoral condyles in flexion, medial meniscus extrusion, and the posteromedial corner for a Baker cyst. Power Doppler for synovial activity. Name on request: quadriceps tendon, suprapatellar pouch, fat pads, femoral cartilage, medial meniscus, medial collateral ligament, pes anserine tendons.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Weight loss (the single most effective disease-modifying measure), quadriceps and general exercise therapy/physiotherapy, topical then oral NSAIDs, TENS, activity pacing, a cane in the contralateral hand, and consideration of a medial off-loader brace for varus alignment.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection - with aspiration of the effusion first when present. Alternatives for the steroid-sparing pathway include viscosupplementation or PRP in appropriate patients; end-stage disease is referred for arthroplasty assessment.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Supine, knee slightly flexed on a roll; high-frequency linear transducer. Longitudinal suprapatellar view; mark the superolateral entry. Prep and drape, gloves, probe cover. In-plane superolateral approach with a 21-23 G needle into the suprapatellar pouch; aspirate effusion first and note its character. Then inject 5 mL (for example triamcinolone 40 mg in 0.25% bupivacaine), confirming free intra-articular flow in real time without resistance.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Septic arthritis - rare but the most serious; emphasize asepsis and post-procedure warning signs; post-injection steroid flare (1-2 days); hemarthrosis; systemic steroid effects including hyperglycemia; possible accelerated cartilage loss with very frequent injections - space injections appropriately.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Pain relief and duration; effusion recurrence; range of motion and function (stairs, walking distance); explicit safety-net advice to report fever or a hot swollen joint immediately; integrate the weight-loss and exercise program; at review, decide on viscosupplementation, repeat injection, or orthopedic referral for end-stage disease. cases.title: Shoulder Pain (Supraspinatus Tendinopathy with Subdeltoid Bursitis)
cases.vignette: A 54-year-old painter reports 5 months of right shoulder pain, worst when working overhead and when lying on the right side at night. He localizes pain to the lateral upper arm. There was no injury. Paracetamol and ibuprofen give partial relief. He is otherwise well and right- hand dominant. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Supraspinatus tendinopathy with subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis (rotator cuff disease) - most likely; partial or full-thickness supraspinatus tear; calcific tendinitis; subacromial impingement; acromioclavicular joint arthrosis; biceps tendinopathy; cervical radiculopathy (C5) with referred pain; adhesive capsulitis if motion is restricted globally.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting with both shoulders exposed. Inspect for deltoid or supraspinatus/infraspinatus fossa atrophy. Palpate the subacromial region and bicipital groove. Active and passive range of motion in all planes - painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction supports impingement; preserved passive motion argues against capsulitis. Special tests: Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement tests; painful arc; Jobe (empty can) test for supraspinatus power; external rotation lag for infraspinatus; lift-off for subscapularis if suspected. Neurological screen with reflex hammer (biceps) and sensation with brush over the C5 dermatome; cervical screen including Spurling to exclude radicular referral.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Shoulder ultrasound now - the first-line test for rotator cuff disease (dynamic, bilateral, radiation-free). Plain radiographs if calcific tendinitis or AC arthrosis is suspected. MRI only if a full-thickness tear requiring surgical opinion is suspected or the diagnosis remains unclear.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview then focused examination, comparing sides. Biceps tendon in the groove (transverse and longitudinal, controlling anisotropy). Subscapularis in external rotation. Supraspinatus in the modified Crass position: assess for hypoechoic thickening, fiber disruption, calcification (bright foci with shadowing for calcific tendinitis) and the subdeltoid bursa above it for fluid or synovial thickening. Measure tendon and bursal findings and compare with the left side. Power Doppler for hyperemia. Dynamic abduction to observe impingement - bursal pooling at the acromial edge. AC joint and posterior recess quickly to complete the protocol. Name on request: biceps tendon, transverse humeral ligament, subscapularis, supraspinatus, subdeltoid bursa, deltoid, acromion, humeral head cartilage.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Activity modification (avoid sustained overhead work), structured physiotherapy with rotator cuff and scapular stabilization strengthening, NSAIDs topical or oral, ice after activity, and relative rest of the painful arc - before any injection.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided subacromial-subdeltoid bursa corticosteroid injection - accurate placement improves outcomes over landmark injection. If a dense calcific deposit is found, ultrasound-guided barbotage (lavage-aspiration) is the procedure of choice.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Sitting or semi-recumbent, hand on the ipsilateral buttock (modified Crass). High- frequency linear transducer in the supraspinatus long axis. Identify the bursa as the hypoechoic interface between deltoid and supraspinatus. Prep, gloves, probe cover. In- plane lateral-to-medial approach with a 22-25 G needle over the tendon into the bursa; inject 3-5 mL (for example triamcinolone 40 mg in lidocaine) watching the bursa separate and fill. No resistance - resistance means intratendinous placement. For barbotage: single- or two-needle lavage of the deposit with saline until the aspirate clears, then bursal steroid.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Post-injection flare (1-2 days); infection; steroid effects (hyperglycemia, skin depigmentation, fat atrophy if placed too superficially); tendon weakening with repeated intratendinous exposure - never inject into the tendon itself; vasovagal reaction; transient increase of impingement pain from bursal distension.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Night pain and painful-arc response within 1-2 weeks; range of motion and Jobe strength; function (overhead work, dressing); reinforce that injection is a window for the strengthening program; review at 4-6 weeks - persistent symptoms warrant repeat imaging for tear progression, repeat injection or barbotage if calcific, and surgical referral for a significant tear.

cases.title: Elbow Pain (Lateral Epicondylosis)
cases.vignette: A 46-year-old office worker and weekend tennis player describes 6 months of right lateral elbow pain, worse with gripping, lifting a coffee cup and turning door handles. She points to the lateral epicondyle. There is no numbness and no neck pain. Physiotherapy and a counterforce brace gave incomplete relief. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Lateral epicondylosis (common extensor tendinosis) - most likely; radial tunnel syndrome/posterior interosseous nerve entrapment (pain more distal, resisted middle- finger extension); radiocapitellar osteoarthritis; lateral collateral ligament injury; cervical radiculopathy (C6) referral; synovial plica.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting, both elbows free. Inspect for swelling; compare forearm circumference. Palpate the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle - point tenderness is expected. Active and passive elbow and wrist range of motion. Special tests: resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended (Cozen) and resisted middle- finger extension reproduce pain; pain on passive wrist flexion with the elbow extended; chair-lift/grip test - weakened painful grip. Neurological screen with reflex hammer (brachioradialis) and sensation with brush; neck screen. Palpate the radial tunnel four fingerbreadths distal to the epicondyle to differentiate PIN entrapment.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Elbow ultrasound now - diagnostic and interventional in one session: tendon thickness, hypoechogenicity, tears, calcification and Doppler hyperemia, compared with the other side. Radiographs if arthritis or loose bodies are suspected. MRI rarely, for refractory cases or pre-surgical planning. No routine laboratory tests.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview of the elbow in four quadrants, then focus laterally. Long-axis and short-axis scans of the common extensor tendon at the lateral epicondyle: look for hypoechoic thickening, loss of the normal fibrillar pattern (controlling anisotropy by toggling), intrasubstance tears, cortical irregularity of the epicondyle, and calcification. Measure tendon thickness and compare with the left side. Power Doppler for neovascularization. Dynamic wrist extension under the probe. Sweep the radiocapitellar joint and the radial nerve. Name on request: common extensor tendon, extensor carpi radialis brevis, lateral epicondyle, radial head, annular ligament, radial nerve.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Load modification and ergonomic changes; eccentric and progressive loading physiotherapy of the wrist extensors; counterforce bracing; topical NSAIDs; avoidance of repetitive gripping during healing - the mainstay, since epicondylosis is a degenerative tendinosis rather than an inflammation.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided dry-needle fenestration (peppering) of the diseased tendon with or without autologous blood or PRP injection - it induces a healing response. Peritendinous corticosteroid gives good short-term relief but poorer long-term outcomes and is now used selectively.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Sitting, elbow flexed and supported, forearm pronated. High-frequency linear transducer in the tendon long axis. Prep, gloves, probe cover. In-plane distal-to- proximal approach with a 22-25 G needle into the area of maximal tendinosis; perform multiple (about 20-30) fenestration passes through the diseased fibers under direct vision to produce controlled microbleeding. Optionally inject 1-2 mL of autologous blood or PRP into the fenestrated tendon. Keep away from the radial nerve anteriorly and do not inject into the lateral collateral ligament complex.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Post-procedure soreness for several days; infection; bleeding/hematoma; radial nerve or posterior interosseous nerve injury if the needle strays anterior; tendon weakening and rupture risk with repeated intratendinous corticosteroid (avoid); skin depigmentation from superficial steroid; vasovagal reaction.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Expected soreness then gradual improvement over 4-12 weeks - tendon healing is slow, counsel accordingly; grip strength and Cozen test at review; adherence to the eccentric loading program (the determinant of long-term success); consider PRP repeat or surgical referral for the small refractory group; watch for signs of instability suggesting collateral ligament injury.

cases.title: Occipital Neuralgia (Cervicogenic Headache)
cases.vignette: A 39-year-old woman presents with 8 months of intermittent shooting pain from the right upper neck into the occipital scalp and behind the right ear, triggered by prolonged desk work and neck extension. Pressing the occipital ridge reproduces her familiar pain. She has no visual symptoms, no nausea and no focal neurological signs. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Greater occipital neuralgia - most likely; cervicogenic headache from the C2-3 facet joint (third occipital nerve); migraine with occipital onset; tension-type headache; myofascial pain of the suboccipital muscles; less likely: C2 radiculopathy, vertebral artery pathology, intracranial causes (screen for red flags).

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting. Inspection of neck posture (forward head). Active and passive cervical range of motion - restricted painful extension/rotation toward the right supports a cervical contribution. Palpate along the superior nuchal line: point tenderness and a Tinel sign over the greater occipital nerve medial to the occipital artery reproducing the shooting pain; palpate the C2-3 facet region. Neurological examination with tools: reflexes (biceps, brachioradialis, triceps) with the hammer; pinprick with toothpick and light touch with brush over the occipital scalp (allodynia/hyperalgesia may be present) and the upper limbs; power and tone. Fundus/fields screening questions for red flags.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: The diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound localizes the nerve and the occipital artery. Cervical spine imaging (radiographs or MRI) only for red flags, trauma or persistent atypical features. A diagnostic greater occipital nerve block is itself the key confirmatory test; if blocks fail, consider third occipital nerve block evaluation for C2-3 facet-mediated pain.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview of the posterior neck with the model sitting and neck slightly flexed. At the superior nuchal line, find the occipital artery with color Doppler - the greater occipital nerve lies just medial to it, a small oval structure between the fascial layers of the trapezius and semispinalis. For the proximal approach, identify the bifid C2 spinous process and slide laterally to find the nerve crossing the obliquus capitis inferior deep to the semispinalis capitis. Compare both sides. Name on request: trapezius, splenius capitis, semispinalis capitis, obliquus capitis inferior, occipital artery, the nerve itself.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Posture and workstation correction; physiotherapy with deep neck flexor training and suboccipital stretching; NSAIDs and neuropathic agents (gabapentin, pregabalin or a tricyclic) for neuralgic pain; heat, massage and trigger-point work; avoidance of sustained neck extension.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided greater occipital nerve block with local anesthetic and corticosteroid - diagnostic and therapeutic, and safer with the occipital artery as a Doppler landmark. Refractory cases may be considered for pulsed radiofrequency of the GON or, if C2-3- mediated, third occipital nerve block followed by radiofrequency.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Sitting, neck flexed over a support; high-frequency linear transducer. Localize the occipital artery with Doppler at the nuchal line and identify the nerve medial to it. Prep, gloves, probe cover. In-plane medial-to-lateral (or lateral-to-medial) approach with a 25 G needle to the perineural plane; hydrodissect around the nerve with 2-3 mL total (for example 0.25% bupivacaine with 10-20 mg triamcinolone), observing spread. The proximal C2-level block under the semispinalis is an alternative target.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Intravascular injection into the occipital artery (minimized by Doppler); transient dizziness or lightheadedness; injection-site pain; alopecia or skin depigmentation at the site from steroid; hematoma; infection; vasovagal reaction; rare allergy.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Immediate concordant relief confirms the diagnosis - record duration against the anesthetic used; headache diary for frequency and intensity over the following weeks; posture and exercise adherence; if relief is significant but temporary, discuss repeat block or pulsed radiofrequency; persistent atypical headaches warrant neurological referral and imaging.

cases.title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (Type I) of the Hand
cases.vignette: A 58-year-old woman presents 4 months after a distal radius fracture (healed, cast removed 6 weeks ago) with persistent burning pain, swelling, shiny red skin and stiffness of the right hand. The hand is warm, exquisitely tender to light touch, and she guards it during washing. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Complex regional pain syndrome type I of the right hand (Budapest criteria: continuing disproportionate pain plus sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema and motor/trophic signs) - most likely; post-traumatic stiffness; median or ulnar neuropathy (carpal tunnel syndrome); infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis); inflammatory arthritis; vascular insufficiency.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Position the model sitting with both hands compared side by side. Inspect for color change, shiny skin, swelling, nail and hair changes, and guarding. Measure and compare hand/finger circumference. Touch gently: allodynia to light brush (use the brush), hyperalgesia to pinprick with the toothpick; assess temperature asymmetry by dorsal hand comparison. Active and passive range of motion of wrist and fingers - stiffness with end-range pain; grip strength (limited by pain). Neurological examination with tools: reflexes and sensation mapping to exclude a defined nerve territory (which would suggest CRPS type II). Check sudomotor signs (sweat asymmetry).

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: CRPS is a clinical diagnosis (Budapest criteria). Three-phase bone scan or MRI can support the diagnosis and exclude occult fracture or infection; radiographs may show patchy osteopenia later. Nerve conduction studies if a defined nerve lesion (type II) is suspected. Ultrasound can assess the median nerve and regional soft tissue and guide the sympathetic block.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Regional overview of the volar wrist and hand soft tissues, comparing sides: skin and subcutaneous thickness, soft-tissue edema, joint effusions and tendon gliding; median nerve CSA at the tunnel inlet to exclude coexisting carpal tunnel syndrome. Then, for the planned intervention, demonstrate the anterior neck at C6: identify the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, thyroid, longus colli muscle and the prevertebral fascia, with color Doppler of the vertebral artery. Name on request: carotid artery, internal jugular vein, longus colli, thyroid, prevertebral fascia, Chassaignac tubercle.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Early aggressive rehabilitation: graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, desensitization, edema management and occupational/physical therapy - the cornerstone; neuropathic agents (gabapentinoids, tricyclics); short-course oral corticosteroid in early florid CRPS; topical agents; vitamin C prophylaxis after wrist fracture as prevention.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided cervical sympathetic trunk (stellate ganglion) block at C6 - both diagnostic of sympathetically maintained pain and therapeutic as a window for rehabilitation. A series is often used; alternatives include repeated blocks, and dorsal column spinal cord stimulation for refractory disease.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Supine with the neck slightly extended; high-frequency linear transducer transverse at C6 (Chassaignac tubercle). Identify carotid artery, internal jugular vein, longus colli and prevertebral fascia; Doppler to exclude the vertebral, inferior thyroidal and ascending cervical vessels. Prep, gloves, probe cover. In-plane lateral-to-medial approach with a 25 G needle to the surface of the longus colli under the prevertebral fascia, medial to the carotid sheath; after negative aspiration inject 3-5 mL of local anesthetic (for example 0.25% bupivacaine) watching spread along the fascia, NOT into the muscle.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Expected Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) and nasal congestion - this is evidence of success, not a complication; hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal spread; difficulty swallowing; hematoma; vertebral artery injection causing seizures; pneumothorax (low placement); neuraxial spread if placed too deep; brachial plexus spread with arm weakness.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Confirm Horner syndrome and ipsilateral hand warming; quantify pain relief, temperature and color change, and allodynia reduction; crucially, exploit each block with immediate physiotherapy and occupational therapy; assess the need for a block series; track hand function (range, grip, swelling) between sessions; escalate to spinal cord stimulation evaluation if blocks give only transient benefit.

cases.title: Sacroiliac Joint Pain
cases.vignette: A 47-year-old man describes 10 months of right-sided low back and buttock pain, maximal just below and medial to the posterior superior iliac spine, sometimes radiating to the posterior thigh. It is worse on prolonged sitting on the right buttock, rising from a chair and climbing stairs. There is no numbness, no morning stiffness beyond 20 minutes, and no red flags. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Sacroiliac joint pain - most likely; lumbar facet syndrome (L4-5, L5-S1); lumbar discogenic pain; L5 or S1 radiculopathy; piriformis syndrome; hip joint pathology; inflammatory sacroiliitis (screen for inflammatory features: prolonged morning stiffness, night pain, alternating buttock pain, family history).

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Observe gait and standing symmetry. Position the model standing then prone and side- lying as tests require. Palpate the PSIS and the sacral sulcus for point tenderness (Fortin finger test - pain within 1 cm inferomedial to the PSIS). Perform the SIJ provocation cluster: distraction, compression (side-lying), thigh thrust, Gaenslen, and FABER (Patrick) - three or more positive supports SIJ pain. Lumbar range of motion; straight leg raise; neurological examination with reflex hammer (patellar, Achilles), sensation with toothpick and brush, and power to exclude radiculopathy; hip examination to exclude hip referral.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Imaging cannot confirm SIJ pain: radiographs/MRI help exclude fracture, spondyloarthropathy or malignancy when indicated (HLA-B27 and inflammatory markers only if sacroiliitis is suspected). The definitive test is an image-guided diagnostic intra-articular SI joint block with concordant relief.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Prone; regional overview of the posterior pelvis with a curvilinear transducer. Start transverse over the median sacral crest, slide laterally to the PSIS; identify the SI joint as the hypoechoic cleft between the sacrum medially and the ilium laterally; trace the cleft to its most caudal (synovial, lower) portion - the injection target. Compare sides. Note depth and angulation for needle planning. Name on request: median sacral crest, PSIS, ilium, sacrum, SI joint cleft, gluteus maximus origin.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Physiotherapy with core, gluteal and pelvic girdle stabilization; manual therapy; activity modification (avoid prolonged asymmetric loading); NSAIDs; SIJ belt for instability patterns; weight management - before escalation to injection.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided SI joint injection (lower synovial portion) with local anesthetic and corticosteroid - diagnostic and therapeutic. For confirmed SIJ pain with temporary response, sacral lateral branch blocks followed by radiofrequency denervation of the posterior joint innervation is the definitive pathway.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Prone; curvilinear transducer transverse over the lower SI joint. Identify the cleft between sacrum and ilium 1-2 cm above its caudal end. Prep, gloves, probe cover. Approach with a 22-25 G needle - out-of-plane (short-axis) or in-plane from medial to lateral - walking the needle off the ilium into the cleft until a subtle give is felt; inject 1- 2 mL (for example 0.25% bupivacaine with 20-40 mg triamcinolone) watching for fluid in the cleft; do not force against bony resistance.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Post-injection soreness; infection; transient sciatic-region paresthesia if injectate tracks anteriorly; intravascular injection; steroid effects (hyperglycemia, flare, depigmentation); failure of intra-articular placement owing to the joint's angulation - confirm with a test injection and two-plane imaging.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Concordant relief within the anesthetic window is the diagnostic endpoint - document it formally; functional change (sitting tolerance, stairs); duration of steroid response; if positive but temporary, proceed to sacral lateral branch blocks and radiofrequency denervation, then reassess at 4-8 weeks; continue the stabilization program throughout.

cases.title: Piriformis Syndrome
cases.vignette: A 50-year-old recreational runner reports 6 months of right buttock pain with intermittent shooting pain down the back of the thigh, worse after long drives and sitting on hard surfaces. Lumbar MRI is normal. Straight leg raise tests elsewhere were reportedly negative. Ibuprofen helps little. You have up to 5 minutes to review this case; you may write notes on this sheet.

qs.q: What are the possible diagnoses (differential diagnosis)?
qs.a: Piriformis syndrome (deep gluteal syndrome with sciatic nerve entrapment) - most likely given the normal MRI; lumbar radiculopathy (L5/S1) despite normal imaging; sacroiliac joint pain; hamstring origin tendinopathy; ischiofemoral impingement; lumbar facet referral; less likely: intrapelvic causes.

qs.q: Please perform examination of your patient.
qs.a: Observe gait; position the model side-lying or prone. Palpate the buttock: tenderness over the piriformis line between the sacrum and the greater trochanter, with reproduction of concordant buttock pain. Special tests: FAIR test (flexion, adduction, internal rotation of the hip) reproducing buttock/sciatic pain; Freiberg sign (pain on forced internal rotation of the extended hip); resisted abduction in the seated position reproducing pain. Hip range of motion; SIJ provocation cluster; neurological examination with tools - reflexes (patellar, Achilles), sensation with toothpick and brush over the L5/S1 dermatomes, and power (typically normal in piriformis syndrome); straight leg raise and slump.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tests should you perform or order, if any?
qs.a: Lumbar MRI already excludes root compression; pelvic MRI or MR neurography if the diagnosis is uncertain or surgery is contemplated. Ultrasound can assess the muscle and guide the diagnostic injection - a piriformis block with concordant relief is the key confirmatory test. EMG/NCS if a neuropathic process must be characterized.

qs.q: Please perform an ultrasound examination.
qs.a: Prone; regional overview of the buttock with a curvilinear transducer. Identify the lateral border of the sacrum and the ilium at the level of the sciatic notch; the piriformis stretches between them deep to the gluteus maximus - confirm by rotating the hip and watching the muscle glide. Locate the sciatic nerve at the infrapiriform fossa (lateral/deep to the muscle) and the inferior gluteal artery with Doppler. Compare muscle bulk and echogenicity with the other side. Name on request: gluteus maximus, piriformis, sacrum, ilium, sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal vessels.

qs.q: What are the best conservative treatment options?
qs.a: Activity modification (avoid prolonged sitting, wallet in back pocket); physiotherapy with piriformis stretching and hip abductor/external rotator strengthening; gait and running-form review; NSAIDs; neuropathic agents if the sciatic component is prominent; heat and manual therapy.

qs.q: What is the best interventional technique?
qs.a: Ultrasound-guided piriformis injection with local anesthetic and corticosteroid - diagnostic and therapeutic. For refractory confirmed cases, botulinum toxin injection of the piriformis or surgical release with sciatic neurolysis are the next steps.

qs.q: Describe the procedure.
qs.a: Prone; curvilinear transducer at the sciatic notch. Identify the piriformis between sacrum and ilium and positively identify the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal artery (Doppler). Prep, gloves, probe cover. In-plane medial-to-lateral approach with a 22-25 G needle into the muscle belly; confirm with a small test injection watching the muscle expand; inject 3-5 mL total (for example 0.25% bupivacaine with 40 mg triamcinolone) distributed within the muscle, keeping the tip away from the sciatic nerve at all times.

qs.q: What are the potential complications or side effects?
qs.a: Sciatic nerve injury (needle or injectate) - the reason for positive nerve identification; transient leg numbness or weakness if local anesthetic reaches the nerve; inferior gluteal artery puncture with hematoma; infection; post-injection buttock soreness; intravascular injection; pudendal structure injury with too-medial placement.

qs.q: What are the major attention points in the post-procedure evaluation?
qs.a: Immediate concordant buttock pain relief (diagnostic endpoint) and any transient leg symptoms before discharge; sitting tolerance and running progression over 4-6 weeks; adherence to the stretching/strengthening program; if the block was positive but temporary, discuss repeat injection versus botulinum toxin; persistent atypical cases deserve MR neurography and surgical opinion.
